column2: On the authority of Muʿādh ibn Jabal (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: “I said: O Messenger of Allah, tell me of a deed that will admit me to Paradise and keep me far from the Fire. He said: You have asked about something great, yet it is easy for the one for whom Allah makes it easy:
worship Allah without associating anything with Him, establish the prayer, give the zakāh, fast Ramaḍān and make pilgrimage to the House. Then he said: Shall I not guide you to the gates of good?

Fasting is a shield; charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire; and a man's prayer in the depth of the night. Then he recited: ‘Their sides forsake their beds…’ until he reached ‘…they used to do’ [al-Sajdah 32:16–17]. Then he said: Shall I not tell you of the head of the matter, its pillar and its highest peak?

I said: Yes indeed, O Messenger of Allah. He said: The head of the matter is Islam, its pillar is the prayer, and its highest peak is jihād—in the path of Allah. Then he said: Shall I not tell you of what holds all of that together?
I said: Yes indeed, O Messenger of Allah. He took hold of his tongue and said: Restrain this. I said: O Prophet of Allah, will we really be taken to account for what we say?
He said: May your mother be bereaved of you, O Muʿādh! Is there anything that topples people on their faces—or he said: on their noses—except the harvests of their tongues?
” Reported by al-Tirmidhī, who said: A ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ hadith.

“You have asked about something great”: about a great deed. Taʿbudu Allāh (“worship Allah”): affirm the oneness of Allah. “The gates of good”: of voluntary deeds. Junnah (“a shield”): a protection for the one who fasts. Al-ṣadaqah (“charity”): voluntary charity, since the obligatory one was mentioned earlier in the hadith.

Tatajāfā (“forsake”): move away from their beds. Al-maḍājiʿ (“beds”): the places where one lies down to sleep. Dhurwah (“highest peak”): the topmost part of anything. “Of what holds all of that together”: its essence and what gathers it.

“Restrain this (kuff ʿalayka)”: restrain from yourself, or in the sense of “confine your tongue”. Thakilatka (“may your mother be bereaved of you”): may your mother lose you; he did not mean it literally—this is a custom of the Arabs. Wa-hal (“is there anything…”): a rhetorical question of denial, in the sense of negation.

Yakubbu (“topples”): throws down. Al-nās (“people”): some of them, a case of using the whole to mean part. “Except the harvests of their tongues”: of speech in which there is no good, but rather harm.
Righteous deeds are a cause of entering Paradise.
Success and guidance are in the hand of Allah the Exalted.
Entering Paradise depends on doing the five pillars of Islam.
The virtue of drawing near to Allah through voluntary deeds after performing the obligations.
Bad deeds are expiated by charity.
The virtue of praying in the depth of the night.
Islam is to the religion as the head is to the body: just as no body remains without a head, no religion is valid except through Islam.
The prayer is to Islam as the pole on which a tent is raised: the tent does not stand upright except by it, and likewise Islam does not stand upright except by establishing the prayer.
The virtue of jihād in the path of Allah, and the virtue of fasting, and that it is a shield that protects and guards the one who fasts.
Restraining and confining the tongue, except in the remembrance of Allah and what brings religious or worldly benefit.
Most of what causes people to enter the Fire is the harvests of the tongues.
The permissibility of an expression of ill-wishing that is not meant literally, if that is understood by the one addressed.

This hadith guides us to the fact that the deed that saves from the Fire and admits to Paradise is worshipping Allah alone and none besides Him, together with carrying out what Allah has made obligatory on the servant of prayer, zakāh, fasting and Ḥajj; that what gathers the various kinds of good is voluntary charity, fasting and the night prayer in the depth of the night;

that the head of the matter is Islam, its pillar is the prayer, and its highest point is jihād to make the word of Allah supreme; and that what holds all of that together is that a person refrains from speech that would spoil these deeds once he has done them.

So let every Muslim who has done righteous deeds beware of letting his tongue loose with what would diminish or nullify them, lest he be among the people of the Fire. We seek refuge with Allah from the Fire and from every [cause of] the Compeller's anger.
Among what has been said about guarding the tongue:
Speak little and seek refuge from its evil; / affliction is tied to some of it.
Guard your tongue and protect yourself from its folly, / until it is as though imprisoned.
Set your heart to watch over your tongue and tell it: / speech is weighed against the two of you.
The printed text reads ينفعها, evidently for ينقصها (“diminish them”), and وكلت, evidently for وكل (“every”).
